title: Logical Conditions
summary: Combine multiple boolean criteria using && (AND), || (OR), and ! (NOT), short-circuit execution, and De Morgan's laws.
learningObjectives: Combine multiple conditional criteria cleanly using logical AND (&&), OR (||), and NOT (!)
Check numeric ranges safely (e.g. min <= x && x <= max)
Leverage short-circuit evaluation to write defensive null checks and zero-checks
Apply De Morgan's laws to simplify convoluted negative conditions
expectedOutcomes: Flatten nested pyramids into elegant single-line compound conditions
Prevent runtime NullPointerExceptions using short-circuit guard patterns

activities.title: Compound Logic: &&, ||, and ! in Decisions

breakdown.whatIsIt: Joining multiple boolean expressions using logical operators to form compound decision gates.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Eliminates messy nested if statements and creates self-documenting business validation rules.
howItWorks: && evaluates left-to-right and short-circuits on first false.
|| evaluates left-to-right and short-circuits on first true.
Compound conditions replace nested ifs with flat readable checks.
keyTakeaways: Never write chained inequalities (10 <= x <= 20); write x >= 10 && x <= 20.
&& requires all true; || requires at least one true.
Short-circuit && prevents NullPointerException when checking objects.
Use parentheses to make operator precedence explicit when mixing && and ||.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Credit Card Eligibility Engine
activities.description: Inspect line 19. Notice how 4 distinct business criteria are combined in a flat, highly readable expression using && and ! without a single nested bracket.

questions.prompt: Why is 'if (10 <= x <= 50)' a compilation error in Java?
options: Java does not support the <= operator
'10 <= x' evaluates to boolean, and boolean cannot be compared with <= 50
x must be declared as a float
questions.explanation: Java evaluates left-to-right: '10 <= x' produces a boolean (true or false). Then 'true <= 50' is invalid because <= requires numbers. The correct syntax is: x >= 10 && x <= 50.
hints: Check the return type of the first comparison.

questions.prompt: What does the expression '!isBlocked && isActive' require for the condition to be true?
options: isBlocked must be true, and isActive must be false
isBlocked must be false, and isActive must be true
questions.explanation: !isBlocked evaluates to true when isBlocked is false. For && to be true, both operands must be true; hence isBlocked is false and isActive is true.

questions.prompt: How does short-circuit evaluation protect: 'if (obj != null && obj.isValid())'?
options: If obj is null, the left side is false, so obj.isValid() is NEVER evaluated, preventing NullPointerException
It makes the method execute asynchronously
It converts null into an empty object
questions.explanation: Because && short-circuits when the left operand is false, the right-hand dereference obj.isValid() is completely skipped when obj == null.
hints: When left is false, && stops immediately.

questions.prompt: In Java operator precedence, which operator has higher precedence: && or ||?
options: They have the exact same precedence
questions.explanation: Logical AND (&&) has higher precedence than Logical OR (||), similar to multiplication over addition. 'A || B && C' is evaluated as 'A || (B && C)'.

questions.prompt: According to De Morgan's Laws, what is the logical equivalent of !(A && B)?
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law states that the negation of an AND is the OR of the negations: !(A && B) == !A || !B.
hints: Negate each condition and flip the operator from AND to OR.

questions.explanation: x < 10 (5 < 10) is true. Because || short-circuits on true, the right-hand operand '++x > 5' is SKIPPED completely! x remains 5.
hints: Short-circuit OR stops as soon as it sees true.

questions.prompt: Which condition correctly verifies that a month number is valid (1 to 12)?
questions.explanation: A valid month must be at least 1 AND at most 12 simultaneously: month >= 1 && month <= 12.
hints: A number can't be >= 1 OR <= 12 (every number is <= 12 or >= 1).

questions.prompt: What does the following condition evaluate to when a = 10, b = 20, c = 30?\n(a > b || b < c) && a < c
questions.explanation: a > b (10 > 20) is false. b < c (20 < 30) is true. So (false || true) is true. Next, a < c (10 < 30) is true. true && true is true.

questions.prompt: What happens if you use the single '&' operator instead of '&&' in: 'if (s != null & s.length() > 0)' when s is null?
options: It throws a NullPointerException because '&' forces both sides to evaluate
questions.explanation: The single '&' is non-short-circuiting; it ALWAYS evaluates both sides. Calling s.length() on null throws NullPointerException.

questions.prompt: How do you test if a character 'c' is an uppercase English letter?
questions.explanation: Characters in Java have underlying Unicode/ASCII numerical codes. 'A' through 'Z' are contiguous, so c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z' checks uppercase.
hints: Character comparisons use character literals in single quotes.

questions.prompt: According to De Morgan's Laws, what is !(A || B) equivalent to?
questions.explanation: The negation of an OR is the AND of the negations: !(A || B) == !A && !B.
hints: Flip OR to AND and negate both sides.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: Logical Conditions

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between && and & when used in conditional statements?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `&&` is the **short-circuit** logical AND operator. If the left-hand operand evaluates to `false`, the right-hand operand is completely skipped because the result is already guaranteed to be false. `&` is the **non-short-circuit** logical operator (and bitwise operator) that always evaluates both operands regardless of the left side. In conditionals, `&&` is almost universally preferred to prevent `NullPointerException` and avoid unnecessary computational overhead.
keyPoints: && short-circuits on false; & always evaluates both operands.

interviewQA.question: Why is operator precedence between && and || a frequent source of bugs?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In Java, `&&` has higher operator precedence than `||` (similar to multiplication having higher precedence than addition). In an expression like `A || B && C`, Java evaluates it as `A || (B && C)`, which may completely contradict the developer's intended logic of `(A || B) && C`. Developers should always use explicit parentheses to remove ambiguity.
keyPoints: && has higher precedence than ||; always use parentheses for clarity.

interviewQA.question: How do De Morgan's laws help in code refactoring?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: De Morgan's laws state that `!(A && B)` is equivalent to `!A || !B`, and `!(A || B)` is equivalent to `!A && !B`. When conditions contain negative logic wrapped in parentheses, applying De Morgan's laws often simplifies the condition into positive, natural expressions that are easier for developers to read and test.
keyPoints: De Morgan's laws simplify complex inverted conditions into readable positive logic.

interviewQA.question: How does short-circuit evaluation enable defensive null checking in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In Java, dereferencing a `null` reference (e.g. `str.length()`) throws a runtime `NullPointerException`. By writing `str != null && str.length() > 0`, if `str` is `null`, the left side is `false`. Because `&&` short-circuits, `str.length()` is never evaluated, completely preventing the exception.
keyPoints: Short-circuit && guarantees null-safety by skipping method calls when references are null.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between || and | in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `||` is the short-circuit logical OR operator that skips the right-hand expression if the left side evaluates to `true`. `|` is the non-short-circuit operator that always evaluates both expressions even if the left side is already `true`.
keyPoints: || short-circuits on true; | always evaluates both operands.

interviewQA.question: Can side-effects inside conditions cause bugs during short-circuiting?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. If an expression includes a mutation like an increment (`if (x > 0 || ++y > 5)`), and the left side is `true`, the right side is skipped, meaning `++y` never executes! Because of this, mutating variables inside conditional expressions is considered a dangerous anti-pattern.
keyPoints: Never mutate variables (++y) inside conditions because short-circuiting can skip the mutation.

interviewQA.question: How do you test if a year is a Leap Year using logical operators?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except for century years which must be divisible by 400: `(year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || (year % 400 == 0)`. Logical operators allow expressing this complete algorithm in a single elegant line.
keyPoints: (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || (year % 400 == 0) represents the standard leap year check.

interviewQA.question: Why is '18 <= age && age <= 60' preferred over 'age >= 18 && age <= 60' by some developers?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Writing `18 <= age && age <= 60` visually mirrors the mathematical range notation $18 \le age \le 60$, placing the variable `age` between its lower and upper boundaries. However, `age >= 18 && age <= 60` is more common in Java style guides. Both are mathematically identical.
keyPoints: Both forms test whether age falls within [18, 60]; consistency in a codebase is key.

interviewQA.question: What is the result of !true && false?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `!true` evaluates to `false`. Then `false && false` evaluates to `false`.
keyPoints: ! has higher precedence than &&, so !true evaluates first.
